Given a relatively projective birational morphism $f\colon X\to Y$ of smoothalgebraic spaces with dimension of fibers bounded by 1, we construct tiltingrelative (over $Y$) generators $T_{X,f}$ and $S_{X,f}$ in $\mathcal{D}^b(X)$.We develop a piece of general theory of strict admissible lattice filtrationsin triangulated categories and show that $\mathcal{D}^b(X)$ has such afiltration $\mathcal{L}$ where the lattice is the set of all birationaldecompositions $f \colon X \xrightarrow{g} Z \xrightarrow{h} Y$ with smooth$Z$. The $t$-structures related to $T_{X,f}$ and $S_{X,f}$ are proved to beglued via filtrations left and right dual to $\mathcal{L}$. An apparatus and method for performing and final forming the winding end turns of a stator. The apparatus includes an elongated arbor on the end of which includes a plurality of radially moveable blades and a cam. A pair of outer diameter jaws is positioned around the end turns whereby the arbor initially can move through the end turns to preform the end turns. After the arbor is moved into position, the end turns are final formed by reducing the volume of the end turn spaces defined by the outer diameter jaws. The coils are final formed by the movement of an end turn heights ring into the end turn spaces defined by the outer diameter jaws.

Intravenous carboplatin for recurrent malignant glioma: a phase II study.Thirty patients with recurrent malignant glioma were treated with intravenous (IV) carboplatin (CBDCA) every 4 weeks at a starting dose of 400 mg/m2 escalating to 450 mg/m2. All patients had documented recurrent tumor after prior radiotherapy but had not received prior chemotherapy. Of 29 assessable patients, four (14%) responded to the treatment for 44, 51+, 72, and 91 weeks; 10 (34%) achieved stable disease (S); while 15 (52%) had progressive disease (P). The total response (responses plus S) rate was 48%, with a median time to progression (MTP) of 26 weeks in these patients; the MTP for all 29 patients was 11 weeks. The toxic effects were mainly hematologic, with thrombocytopenia and granulocytopenia being mild at 400 mg/m2 and 450 mg/m2 doses. NO neurotoxicity or renal toxicity was encountered. These results suggest that CBCDA given at 400 mg/m2 or 450 mg/m2 every 4 weeks is marginally active in patients with recurrent malignant gliomas. Since hematologic toxicity is mild, a higher dose could possibly be given, and may increase the response rate.

We show that a deep-learning neural network potential (DP) based on densityfunctional theory (DFT) calculations can well describe Cu-Zr materials, anexample of a binary alloy system that can coexist in several orderedintermetallics and as an amorphous phase. The complex phase diagram for Cu-Zrmakes it a challenging system for traditional atomistic force-fields that failto describe well the different properties and phases. Instead, we show that aDP approach using a large database with ~300k configurations can render resultsgenerally on par with DFT. The training set includes configurations of pristineand bulk elementary metals and intermetallics in the liquid and solid phases inaddition to slab and amorphous configurations. The DP model was validated bycomparing bulk properties such as lattice constants, elastic constants, bulkmoduli, phonon spectra, surface energies to DFT values for identicalstructures. Further, we contrast the DP results with values obtained usingwell-established two embedded atom method potentials. Overall, our DP potentialprovides near DFT accuracy for the different Cu-Zr phases but with a fractionof its computational cost, thus enabling accurate computations of realisticatomistic models especially for the amorphous phase.

[Stearoyl-CoA desaturase--the lipid metabolism regulator].Stearoyl-CoA desaturase is an enzyme from the class of oxidoreductase, which catalyzes the formation of a fatty acid double bond between C9 and C10. It plays a key role in composition of the fatty acid profile in adipose tissue and animal products such as meat and milk. Additionally, it is an important regulator of metabolic processes in the body, and it determines the maintenance of energy homeostasis. This enzyme is encoded by an SCD gene, which, depending on the species, may exist as different isoforms. mRNA expression of stearoyl-CoA desaturase is dependent on many factors, including diet, hormones, and the activity of other genes. In previous studies, several mutations were characterized within the sequence of Δ9-desaturase, which may affect the activity of the protein in the tissues, as well as the value of breeding animals. Effects of particular mutations of the gene encoding the enzyme appears to be particularly important for diseases associated with obesity, diabetes, hypertension, heart diseases or cancer in humans. Also, it seems that using sheep as a potential animal model could be helpful in uncovering and understanding the mechanisms regulated by stearoyl-CoA desaturase.

Bayesian methods of matrix factorization (MF) have been actively explored recently as promising alternatives to classical singular value decomposition. In this paper, we show that, despite the fact that the optimization problem is non-convex, the global optimal solution of variational Bayesian (VB) MF can be computed analytically by solving a quartic equation. This is highly advantageous over a popular VBMF algorithm based on iterated conditional modes since it can only find a local optimal solution after iterations. We further show that the global optimal solution of empirical VBMF (hyperparameters are also learned from data) can also be analytically computed. We illustrate the usefulness of our results through experiments.

A primer composition for adhering a topcoat to a flexible plastic substrate includes a blend of acrylic and urethane resins, and pigments dispersed in a water based solvent system. About 10 to about 20 percent of the resins are polyurethene by weight, the balance of the resins consisting essentially of acrylic polymers. The composition consists of from about 15 to 30 percent resins, and from about 20 to about 35 percent pigments by weight, and has a total solids content of from about 35 to about 70 percent. The water based solvent system is primarily water, but contains water-miscible organic components which provide for rapid drying, and good coalescing and film forming properties, while minimizing volatile organic content. The compositions dry rapidly at ambient conditions upon application to flexible plastic substrates to provide a continuous, flexible film which exhibits excellent adhesion with the substrate and with subsequently applied topcoats.

We study theoretically, via Monte Carlo simulations on lattices containing upto 1000 x 1000 spins, thermal creation of skyrmion lattices in a 2Dferromagnetic film with perpendicular magnetic anisotropy andDzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction. At zero temperature, skyrmions only appearin the magnetization process in the presence of static disorder. Thermalfluctuations violate conservation of the topological charge and reduce theeffective magnetic anisotropy that tends to suppress skyrmions. In accordancewith recent experiments, we find that elevated temperatures assist theformation of skyrmion structures. Once such a structure is formed, it can befrozen into a regular skyrmion lattice by reducing the temperature. Weinvestigate topological properties of skyrmion structures and find the averageskyrmion size. Energies of domain and skyrmion states are computed. It is shownthat skyrmion lattices have lower energy than labyrinth domains within a narrowfield range.

We study the Dine-Fischler-Srednicki (DFS) model in the light of the recentHiggs LHC results and electroweak precision data. The DFS model is a naturalextension of the two-Higgs doublet model endowed with a Peccei-Quinn symmetryand leading to a physically acceptable axion. For generic couplings, the modelreproduces the minimal Standard Model showing only tiny deviations (extremedecoupling scenario) whereas all additional degrees of freedom (with theexception of the axion) are very heavy. Recently, new corners of this modelhave been highlighted where it may exhibit enlarged global symmetries makingthe corresponding models technically natural (naturalness scenario). In somecases an additional Higgs could be present at the weak scale. In this case, thenew light $0^+$ state would be accompanied by relatively light charged andneutral pseudoscalar Higgses. We will use the oblique corrections, particularly$\Delta\rho$, to constrain the mass spectrum in this case. As a final result,we also work out the non-linear parametrization of the DFS model in the genericcase where all scalars except the lightest Higgs and the axion have masses ator beyond the TeV scale.

Multiplex networks offer an important tool for the study of complex systemsand extending techniques originally designed for single--layer networks is animportant area of study. One of the most important methods for analyzingnetworks is clustering the nodes into communities that represent commonconnectivity patterns. In this paper we extend spectral clustering to multiplexstructures and discuss some of the difficulties that arise in attempting todefine a natural generalization. In order to analyze our approach, we describethree simple, synthetic multiplex networks and compare the performance ofdifferent multiplex models. Our results suggest that a dynamically motivatedmodel is more successful than a structurally motivated model in discovering theappropriate communities.

We analytically compute the long-term orbital variations of a test particleorbiting a central body acted upon by an incident monochromatic planegravitational wave. We assume that the characteristic size of the perturbedtwo-body system is much smaller than the wavelength of the wave. Moreover, wealso suppose that the wave's frequency is much smaller than the particle'sorbital one. We make neither a priori assumptions about the direction of thewavevector nor on the orbital geometry of the planet. We find that, while thesemi-major axis is left unaffected, the eccentricity, the inclination, thelongitude of the ascending node, the longitude of pericenter and the meananomaly undergo non-vanishing long-term changes. They are not secular trendsbecause of the slow modulation introduced by the tidal matrix coefficients andby the orbital elements themselves. They could be useful to indepenedentlyconstrain the ultra-low frequency waves which may have been indirectly detectedin the BICEP2 experiment. Our calculation holds, in general, for anygravitationally bound two-body system whose characteristic frequency is muchlarger than the frequency of the external wave. It is also valid for a genericperturbation of tidal type with constant coefficients over timescales of theorder of the orbital period of the perturbed particle.

The mathematics that led to the discovery by Asst Prof Tsang and his teamResearchers from NUS Electrical and Computer Engineering have discovered new optical techniques that enable separation between two light sources to be measured more precisely than current approaches. These techniques could potentially improve the resolution of microscopes and telescopes by orders of magnitude. Conventional methods of imaging often experience blurring and noise due to the wave and particle nature of light. This problem particularly hinders the study of fluorescent particles in microscopy and binary stars in astronomy.The study, conducted by Assistant Professor Tsang Man Kei and his research fellows Dr Ranjith Nair and Dr Xiao-Ming Lu, used a theory called quantum metrology. Their calculations revealed that cleverer quantum optical methods can extract the full information contained in two typical light sources about their separation, allowing it to be more accurately measured.The work was published in Physical Review X on 29 August 2016.Read the full article.

Diversified retrieval and online learning are two core research areas in the design of modern information retrieval systems.In this paper, we propose the linear submodular bandits problem, which is an online learning setting for optimizing a general class of feature-rich submodular utility models for diversified retrieval. We present an algorithm, called LSBGREEDY, and prove that it efficiently converges to a near-optimal model. As a case study, we applied our approach to the setting of personalized news recommendation, where the system must recommend small sets of news articles selected from tens of thousands of available articles each day. In a live user study, we found that LSBGREEDY significantly outperforms existing online learning approaches.

Inter-observer reliability of digital vaginal examination using a four-grade scale in different patient positions.This study aims to compare digital vaginal examination with the patient in supine and standing position and to correlate the degree of pelvic organ prolapse (POP) with a prolapse quality of life (P-QOL) questionnaire. Two hundred and seven women with POP symptoms were digitally examined in supine and standing positions using a four-grade scale (none, minimal, moderate, and severe). P-QOL was used to assess the severity of prolapse symptoms. Cohen's kappa coefficient was used to calculate the inter-observer agreement and Spearman rank correlation test to assess the correlation between examination findings and P-QOL scores. Only vaginal examination findings in standing position had a good inter-observer reliability (kappa value 0.76-0.91). The severity of P-QOL scores only correlated with the examination findings in the standing position (P < 0.001). Digital examination of POP is unreliable if woman is supine but is reliable and correlates with symptoms and QOL impairment when the examination is performed with the patient standing.

Breastfeeding and Childhood Cancer: Is Breastfeeding Preventative to Childhood Cancer?Breastfeeding is well-known to have a protective effect against infection in infants. It has been suggested that breast milk may play a role in the prevention of certain childhood cancer. We investigated this issue in a case-control study comprising 300 patients with childhood cancer. There was 73 patients (24.3%) with leukemia, 82 patients (27.3%) with lymphoma, and 146 patients (48.4%) with solid tumors (brain tumors, neuroblastoma, soft tissue sarcomas, germ cell tumors, renal tumor, bone tumor, retinoblastoma, hepatoblastoma, and others) and 316 controls matched for age and sex. Breastfeeding duration of the control group was found to be significantly longer than the patient group (X(2) = 57.774; P < .001). In conclusion, breastfeeding was found to be inversely associated with pediatric cancer in our study.

Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board is consulting on plans to withdraw consultant-led maternity care at one of three district hospitals. Earlier plans to downgrade services at Glan Clwyd Hospital in Bodelwyddan, Denbighshire, were sent back to the drawing board after public outcry. The proposed changes stem from a shortage of doctors. Health bosses still favour downgrading services at the hospital and earlier this month the board agreed to start a fresh public consultation on those plans and others. Alternatives include withdrawing doctor-led maternity care at hospitals in Bangor or Wrexham, or they could agree to make no changes meaning consultant-led care would remain at all three hospitals. Those against the plans say expectant mothers who need care from doctors would be put at greater risk by having to travel further for treatment. The British Medical Association and politicians have also previously criticised the health board for not seeking the views of staff and the public in drawing up its plans. A final decision is expected in November.

We present an isolated Milky Way-like simulation in GADGET2 N-body SPH code.The Galactic disk star formation rate (SFR) surface densities and stellar massindicative of Solar neighbourhood are used as thresholds to model thedistribution of stellar mass in life friendly environments. SFR and stellarcomponent density are calculated averaging the GADGET2 particle properties on a2D grid mapped on the Galactic plane. The peak values for possibly habitablestellar mass surface density move from $10$ to $15$ kpc cylindricalgalactocentric distance in $10$ Gyr simulated time span. At $10$ Gyr thesimulation results imply the following. Stellar particles which have spentalmost all of their life time in habitable friendly conditions reside typicallyat $\sim16$ kpc from Galactic centre and are $\sim 3$ Gyr old. Stellarparticles that have spent $\ge 90 \%$ of their $4-5$ Gyr long life time inhabitable friendly conditions, are also predominantly found in the outskirts ofthe Galactic disk. Less then $1 \%$ of these particles can be found at atypical Solar system galactocentric distance of $8-10$ kpc. Our results implythat the evolution of an isolated spiral galaxy is likely to result in galacticcivilizations emerging at the outskirts of the galactic disk around stellarhosts younger than the Sun.

This report describes the design of a programmable general purpose analog neural computer and simulator. It is intended primarily for real-world real-time computations such as analysis of visual or acoustical patterns, robotics and the development of special purpose neural nets. The machine is scalable and composed of interconnected modules containing arrays of neurons, modifiable synapses and switches. It runs entirely in analog mode but connection architecture, synaptic gains and time constants as well as neuron parameters are set digitally. Each neuron has a limited number of inputs and can be connected to any but not all other neurons. For the determination of synaptic gains and the implementation of learning algorithms the neuron outputs are multiplexed, AID converted and stored in digital memory. Even at moderate size of 1()3 to IDS neurons computational speed is expected to exceed that of any current digital computer.

A precompression system for a liquid dispensing device is presented, that prevents liquid from being discharged until a predetermined pressure has been built up. The system comprises a pump for drawing liquid through an inlet and discharging it through an outlet, and a precompression valve disposed between the pump and the outlet. The valve allows liquid in the pump to reach the outlet once the predetermined pressure is established, and stops liquid from reaching the outlet once the pressure falls below it. The precompression valve comprises an elastic diaphragm normally closing the valve opening, with a concave surface facing the valve opening and in fluid communication with the pump and a convex surface in fluid communication with atmospheric pressure. The diaphragm may be stretched around a valve seat. Methods of assembling such a precompression system in a dispensing device are also presented.

We have investigated shear viscosity of quark matter in presence of a stronguniform magnetic field background where Nambu-Jona-Lasinio model has beenconsidered to describe the magneto-thermodynamical properties of the medium. Inpresence of magnetic field, shear viscosity coefficient gets split intodifferent components because of anisotropy in tangential stress of the fluid.Four different components can be merged to two components in limit of strongfield, where collisional width of quark becomes much lower than its synchrotronfrequency. A simplified contact diagram of quark-quark interaction can estimatea small collisional width, where strong field limit expressions are exactlyapplicable. Although, for RHIC or LHC matter, one can expect a large thermalwidth, for which generalized four components viscosities are necessary. We haveexplored these all different possible cases in the thermodynamical framework ofNambu-Jona-Lasinio model.

In dilute gas kinetic theory, model collision dynamics such asBhatnagar-Gross-Krook (BGK) model is often used to get a better insight andnumerical modelling. BGK model and its variants assume that highly nonlinearcollision term can be replaced by a simple relaxation dynamics towardsMaxwell-Boltzmann distribution. Lebowitz et al., proposed an alternativeframework for the collision model, known as Fokker-Planck model, where therelaxation of an arbitrary distribution towards Maxwell-Boltzmann distributionis modelled as a drift-diffusion process in velocity space. In the presentmanuscript, we extend the single component Fokker-Planck model to a binary gasmixture model over a large range of Schmidt numbers. We prove that thesemixture models satisfy the necessary conservation laws and the H-theorem.

While previous distribution shift detection approaches can identify if a shift has occurred, these approaches cannot localize which specific features have caused a distribution shift---a critical step in diagnosing or fixing any underlying issue. For example, in military sensor networks, users will want to detect when one or more of the sensors has been compromised, and critically, they will want to know which specific sensors might be compromised. Thus, we first define a formalization of this problem as multiple conditional distribution hypothesis tests and propose both non-parametric and parametric statistical tests. For both efficiency and flexibility, we then propose to use a test statistic based on the density model score function (\ie gradient with respect to the input)---which can easily compute test statistics for all dimensions in a single forward and backward pass. Any density model could be used for computing the necessary statistics including deep density models such as normalizing flows or autoregressive models. We additionally develop methods for identifying when and where a shift occurs in multivariate time-series data and show results for multiple scenarios using realistic attack models on both simulated and real-world data.

Automatic discovery of category-specific 3D keypoints from a collection ofobjects of some category is a challenging problem. One reason is that not allobjects in a category necessarily have the same semantic parts. The level ofdifficulty adds up further when objects are represented by 3D point clouds,with variations in shape and unknown coordinate frames. We define keypoints tobe category-specific, if they meaningfully represent objects' shape and theircorrespondences can be simply established order-wise across all objects. Thispaper aims at learning category-specific 3D keypoints, in an unsupervisedmanner, using a collection of misaligned 3D point clouds of objects from anunknown category. In order to do so, we model shapes defined by the keypoints,within a category, using the symmetric linear basis shapes without assuming theplane of symmetry to be known. The usage of symmetry prior leads us to learnstable keypoints suitable for higher misalignments. To the best of ourknowledge, this is the first work on learning such keypoints directly from 3Dpoint clouds. Using categories from four benchmark datasets, we demonstrate thequality of our learned keypoints by quantitative and qualitative evaluations.Our experiments also show that the keypoints discovered by our method aregeometrically and semantically consistent.

I found this second volume of Farley Mowat's TOP OF THE WORLD TRILOGY even more readable that the first. This one deals almost exclusively with the efforts of people to get further and further north, culminating in attempts to reach the North Pole.What makes these accounts different from the others available is its reliance on presenting the stories in the words of the participants. Most of the reading is from the accounts of the explorers themselves. Mowat simply throws in an introduction, occasional comments for each narrative and an epilog for each venture.With this style of presentation, the story is of necessity selective. A process and a set of equipment for reactivating spent activated carbon onto which pollutants were adsorbed. The equipment includes (A) a mixing tank for mixing given amounts of water, ethanol and sodium hydroxide solution which are supplied from the respective receptacles thereof; (B) a reactivation reactor for receiving the mixed solution from the mixing tank and subjecting the spent activated carbon filled therein to the mixed solution to effect the desorption of the pollutants adsorbed on the spent activated carbon, wherein the reactivation reactor includes a unit for regulating temperature of the mixed solution; and (C) a storage tank for receiving the reactivated carbon.

We present the results of an analytical and numerical study of the long-timebehavior for certain Fermi-Pasta-Ulam (FPU) lattices viewed as perturbations ofthe completely integrable Toda lattice. Our main tools are the direct andinverse scattering transforms for doubly-infinite Jacobi matrices, which arewell-known to linearize the Toda flow. We focus in particular on the evolutionof the associated scattering data under the perturbed vs. the unperturbedequations. We find that the eigenvalues present initially in the scatteringdata converge to new, slightly perturbed eigenvalues under the perturbeddynamics of the lattice equation. To these eigenvalues correspond solitarywaves that emerge from the solitons in the initial data. We also find that neweigenvalues emerge from the continuous spectrum as the lattice system is let toevolve under the perturbed dynamics.

As is known in the art, a quantity of compacted crop material is encircled with a length of twine, or similar binding material, and a knot is tied in primary and secondary portions thereof to produce a discrete package of material. The improved knotter includes a rotatable twine holder for gripping the primary and secondary portions of twine and holding them in a side-by-side relationship extending along a predetermined path. A rotatable billhook is mounted adjacent the twine holder and positioned to intersect the predetermined path. Drive means interconnecting the twine holder and billhook rotate the two elements in timed relation such that during a first cycle of the billhook the twine portions are positioned thereabout, and during a second cycle of the billhook a knot is tied therein.

We study theoretically, via Monte Carlo simulations on lattices containing upto 1000 x 1000 spins, thermal creation of skyrmion lattices in a 2Dferromagnetic film with perpendicular magnetic anisotropy andDzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction. At zero temperature, skyrmions only appearin the magnetization process in the presence of static disorder. Thermalfluctuations violate conservation of the topological charge and reduce theeffective magnetic anisotropy that tends to suppress skyrmions. In accordancewith recent experiments, we find that elevated temperatures assist theformation of skyrmion structures. Once such a structure is formed, it can befrozen into a regular skyrmion lattice by reducing the temperature. Weinvestigate topological properties of skyrmion structures and find the averageskyrmion size. Energies of domain and skyrmion states are computed. It is shownthat skyrmion lattices have lower energy than labyrinth domains within a narrowfield range.

Impact for iOSI know you're waiting for the release of the Impact Game Engine, and I promise you, it's coming. I just get distracted too easily. So here's my game Biolab Disaster running on the iPhone 3GS with 60 frames per second:The game is running in its own process and is not using the iPhone's browser at all. Instead, it's just using the JavaScriptCore Framework to run the game. All the necessary calls to the Canvas API have been reimplemented with OpenGL-ES and the touch input is passed over to JavaScript to be evaluated by the engine. I of course had to make some changes to the engine, but the game source code is exactly the same as for the web version.The JavaScriptCore Framework is still private on iOS. So as it is now, I won't be allowed to distribute the game in the AppStore. But my understanding is, that if I bundle my own copy of the JavaScriptCore Framework (which is part of WebKit and thus freely available) with my game, I should be on the safe side. Let's see how this works out.

The proton radius conundrum [R. Pohl et al., Nature vol.466, p.213 (2010) andA. Antognini et al., Science vol.339, p.417 (2013)] highlights the need torevisit any conceivable sources of electron-muon nonuniversality inlepton-proton interactions within the Standard Model. Superficially, a numberof perturbative processes could appear to lead to such a nonunversality. One ofthese is a coupling of the scattered electron into an electronic as opposed toa muonic vacuum polarization loop in the photon exchange of two valence quarks,which is present only for electron projectiles as opposed to muon projectiles.However, we can show that this effect actually is part of the radiativecorrection to the proton's polarizability contribution to the Lamb shift,equivalent to a radiative correction to double scattering. We conclude that anyconceivable genuine nonuniversality must be connected with a nonperturbativefeature of the proton's structure, e.g., with the possible presence of lightsea fermions as constituent components of the proton. If we assume an averageof roughly 0.7*10^(-7) light sea positrons per valence quark, then we can showthat virtual electron-positron annihiliation processes lead to an extra term inthe electron-proton versus muon-proton interaction, which has the right signand magnitude to explain the proton radius discrepancy.

Deactivation and Regeneration of NaTaO3 Photocatalyst in Cooperating Dehydrogenation Coupling of Isopropanol and Hydrogenation Coupling of Acetone Reaction System.Photocatalyst activity is influenced by many factors, such as adsorption of by-products, runoff of surface hydroxyl groups and carriers. In this study, a simple and efficient photocatalyst regeneration method was developed. Results indicated that NaTaO3 photocatalyst lost its photoactivity after three cycles of reaction that involves coupling of isopropanol and hydrogenation coupling of acetone reaction system. Runoff of Na on the surface was the main reason for the deactivation of NaTaO3 photocatalyst. After hydrothermal treatment of the deactivated NaTaO3 with 10 m NaOH at 180°C for 12 h, its photocatalytic activity was restored to the original level. The photocatalytic activity remained stable even after 10 cycles.

Cattani-Sassone's notion of higher dimensional transition system isinterpreted as a small-orthogonality class of a locally finitely presentabletopological category of weak higher dimensional transition systems. Inparticular, the higher dimensional transition system associated with thelabelled n-cube turns out to be the free higher dimensional transition systemgenerated by one n-dimensional transition. As a first application of thisconstruction, it is proved that a localization of the category of higherdimensional transition systems is equivalent to a locally finitely presentablereflective full subcategory of the category of labelled symmetric precubicalsets. A second application is to Milner's calculus of communicating systems(CCS): the mapping taking process names in CCS to flows is factorized throughthe category of higher dimensional transition systems. The method also appliesto other process algebras and to topological models of concurrency other thanflows.

The last two decades have seen a growing trend towards the experimentalefforts at the electron-proton collider HERA in which have collected highprecision data on the spectrum of leading neutron (LN) and leading-proton (LP)carrying a large fraction of the proton's energy. In our recent study [Phys.Rev. D \textbf{95} (2017), 074011], we have proposed an approach based on theFractures Functions (FF) formalism and have extracted the neutron FractureFunctions (neutron FFs) from a global QCD analysis of LN production datameasured by H1 and ZEUS collaborations at HERA. We have shown that consideringthe approach based on the framework of Fracture Functions, one couldphenomenologically parametrize the neutron FFs at the input scale. In order toaccess the uncertainties for the obtained neutron FFs as well as the LNstructure functions and cross section, associated with the uncertainties in thedata, we have made an extensive use of the "Hessian method". Our theorypredictions based on the obtained neutron FFs are in satisfactory agreementwith all LN data analyzed, for a wide range of $\beta$ and $x_L$.

Computing the inverse dynamics of a robot ann is an active area of research in the control literature. We hope to learn the inverse dynamics by training a neural network on the measured response of a physical ann. The input to the network is a temporal window of measured positions; output is a vector of torques. We train the network on data measured from the first two joints of the CMU Direct-Drive Arm II as it moves through a randomly-generated sample of "pick-and-place" trajectories. We then test generalization with a new trajectory and compare its output with the torque measured at the physical arm. The network is shown to generalize with a root mean square error/standard deviation (RMSS) of 0.10. We interpreted the weights of the network in tenns of the velocity and acceleration filters used in conventional control theory.

Pyrrolizidine alkaloids from Symphytum officinale L. and their percutaneous absorption in rats.An analysis of a commercial sample of Symphyti radix originating from Poland with a total alkaloid content of 0.07% revealed the presence of 7 pyrrolizidine alkaloid-N-oxides: 7-acetyl intermedine, 7-acetyl lycopsamine as the main constituents and lycopsamine, intermedine, symphytine and traces of 2 further not yet identified alkaloids. The percutaneous absorption of these alkaloids was investigated in rats, using a crude alcoholic extract of the plant corresponding to a dose of 194 mg alkaloid-N-oxides/kg b.wt. The excretion of N-oxides in the urine during 2 days was in the range of 0.1-0.4% of the dose. The dermally absorbed N-oxides are not or only to a small extent converted to the free alkaloids in the organism. The oral application led to a 20-50 times higher excretion of N-oxides and free alkaloids in the urine.

In a digital FM receiver having a demodulator that receives a radio signal and generates therefrom a phase sample whose behavior determines an output of the demodulator, an apparatus for removing a low-frequency interference signal from the phase sample converts the phase sample into a frequency sample which is then high-pass filtered to produce a filtered frequency sample. The filtered frequency sample is then converted into a filtered phase sample, which may be further demodulated in accordance with known techniques. Converting the phase sample into a frequency sample may be performed by a first order difference circuit. Converting the filtered frequency sample into the filtered phase sample may be performed by an integrator. An apparatus and method for performing and final forming the winding end turns of a stator. GFP transgenic animals in biomedical research: a review of potential disadvantages.Green Fluorescent protein (GFP) transgenic animals are accepted tools for studying various physiological processes, including organ development and cell migration. However, several in vivo studies claimed that GFP may impair transgenic animals' health. Glomerulosclerosis was observed in transgenic mice and rabbits with ubiquitous reporter protein expression. Heart-specific GFP expression evoked dilated cardiomyopathy and altered cardiac function in transgenic mouse and zebrafish lines, respectively. Moreover, growth retardation and increased axon swelling were observed in GFP and yellow fluorescent protein (YFP) transgenic mice, respectively. This review will focus on the potential drawbacks of the applications of GFP transgenic animals in biomedical research.

An array of bent wire connectors to grip the edge of a printed circuit board is held in spaced, opposed grooves on facing side walls of a holder so that the whole array can be affixed to a mother board as a unit by soldering the free ends of the connectors in place. The grooves can be preformed to hold the connectors in the array, or they can be formed in situ by heating a jig with the connectors assembled in a similar array of holes in the surface of the jig and then pressing a thermoplastic holder onto the connectors. The heated connectors soften the contiguous portions of the holder, and after the latter is in place, the assembly is allowed to cool so that the thermoplastic material can reharden in gripping relation to the connectors. A bar can separate gripping portions of the connectors to align them and give them a pre-set position to receive the edge of the printed circuit board easily.

Unsupervised domain adaption aims to learn a powerful classifier for thetarget domain given a labeled source data set and an unlabeled target data set.To alleviate the effect of `domain shift', the major challenge in domainadaptation, studies have attempted to align the distributions of the twodomains. Recent research has suggested that generative adversarial network(GAN) has the capability of implicitly capturing data distribution. In thispaper, we thus propose a simple but effective model for unsupervised domainadaption leveraging adversarial learning. The same encoder is shared betweenthe source and target domains which is expected to extract domain-invariantrepresentations with the help of an adversarial discriminator. With the labeledsource data, we introduce the center loss to increase the discriminative powerof feature learned. We further align the conditional distribution of the twodomains to enforce the discrimination of the features in the target domain.Unlike previous studies where the source features are extracted with a fixedpre-trained encoder, our method jointly learns feature representations of twodomains. Moreover, by sharing the encoder, the model does not need to know thesource of images during testing and hence is more widely applicable. Weevaluate the proposed method on several unsupervised domain adaption benchmarksand achieve superior or comparable performance to state-of-the-art results.

We investigate thermalization dynamics of a driven dipolar many-body quantum system through the stability of discrete time crystalline order. Using periodic driving of electronic dipoles in a two-dimensional array, our research team aimed to uncover the underlying mechanisms governing the emergence of coherent structures in interacting quantum systems. By carefully tuning the intensity and frequency of the driving field, we observed a fascinating transition from a disordered to a crystalline state, marked by the formation of discrete time crystals.As we probed the system's behavior under varying driving conditions, we discovered that the stability of the time crystal was directly linked to the system's ability to thermalize. Our findings suggest that the interplay between periodic driving and many-body interactions gives rise to a unique regime, where the system's dynamics are dictated by the interplay between disorder and order. This breakthrough has significant implications for our understanding of quantum thermalization and the potential applications of driven quantum systems in quantum technologies.

Fast pyrolysis characteristics of two typical coastal zone biomass fuels by thermal gravimetric analyzer and down tube reactor. This study aimed at investigating fast pyrolysis behavior of seaweed and mangrove, two common coastal biomasses. We used a thermal gravimetric analyzer to track weight loss and a down tube reactor to simulate real-world pyrolysis conditions.Turns out, seaweed goes up in flames quicker than you can say "beach bonfire," hitting its peak decomposition rate around 300°C. On the other hand, mangrove wood takes its sweet time, with a more gradual weight loss up to 400°C. Both biomasses produced a decent amount of bio-oil, but seaweed's was a bit runnier – think of it as the difference between syrup and honey.This research not only sheds light on the pyrolysis dynamics of these coastal fuels but also hints at their potential in sustainable energy production. Who knew beach clean-ups could lead to green energy?

We report the study of metal-STO-metal memristors where the doping concentration in STO (strontium titanate) can be fine-tuned through electric field migration of oxygen. This investigation focuses on the resistive switching behavior of these devices, which is critical for advancing non-volatile memory and neuromorphic computing technologies. By applying an external electric field, oxygen vacancies within the STO lattice are manipulated, enabling precise control over the material's electrical properties. This process allows for the modulation of the memristor's resistance states, offering a pathway to achieve high-performance, low-power devices.Our experiments demonstrate that the migration of oxygen vacancies under an electric field leads to stable and reproducible resistive switching. The ability to fine-tune the doping concentration in STO provides a versatile platform for designing memristive devices with tailored characteristics. These findings highlight the potential of metal-STO-metal memristors for next-generation electronic applications, emphasizing their scalability and compatibility with existing semiconductor fabrication processes. This study contributes to the growing body of research aimed at harnessing oxide-based materials for advanced computing and memory solutions.

The foundation for the Internet was established by the U.S. Department of Defence in the 1960s, a period marked by the development of early computer networks. This era saw the creation of ARPANET, a precursor to the modern Internet, which facilitated the sharing of information among Department of Defence sites. ARPANET's key innovation was its ability to transmit data packets, allowing for the splitting, forwarding, and reconstruction of information across distant sites. This mechanism, known as the Transmission Control Protocol/Network (TCP/N), was a revolutionary advancement in networking, enabling the seamless exchange of data.ARPANET's development was initially intended for military use, yet its architecture laid the groundwork for the global communication networks that we rely on today. Over time, ARPANET expanded, becoming a platform for academic and commercial networks, ultimately evolving into the Internet as we know it. The Department of Defence's contributions in the 1960s were pivotal in establishing the principles that form the backbone of the Internet, highlighting the importance of early collaborative efforts in shaping this global infrastructure.

**New Insight into Phase Equilibria Involving Imidazolium Bistriflamide Ionic Liquids and Their Mixtures with Alcohols and Water** The fluid phase equilibria of imidazolium bistriflamide ionic liquids (ILs) and their mixtures with alcohols and water have been the focus of groundbreaking research, offering new insights into their thermodynamic behavior and potential applications. A recent study has revealed intricate details about the phase transitions and solubility patterns of these systems, which are critical for advancing their use in green chemistry, catalysis, and separation processes. Researchers found that the unique hydrogen-bonding interactions between imidazolium cations, bistriflamide anions, and polar solvents like water and alcohols significantly influence phase stability. The study highlights how varying alkyl chain lengths on the imidazolium cation affect miscibility and phase separation, with shorter chains favoring greater solubility in water and longer chains enhancing compatibility with alcohols. These findings could pave the way for optimizing IL-based solvents in industrial applications, such as CO2 capture and biomass processing, where precise control over phase behavior is essential. The research underscores the importance of understanding molecular interactions in designing sustainable and efficient chemical systems.

Urodynamic correlates of resolution of reflux in meningomyelocele patients. Resolution of reflux in meningomyelocele patients is a reflection of improved urodynamic function, as evidenced by studies showing that successful treatment of reflux often correlates with normalization of bladder dynamics. Urodynamic evaluation provides critical insights into the underlying mechanisms of reflux and guides the selection of appropriate therapeutic interventions. For instance, careful monitoring of bladder pressure, residual volume, and flow patterns helps identify optimal Candidates for surgical or medical therapies. Furthermore, the resolution of reflux is not merely a physiological consequence of treatment but a testament to the restoration of normal urinary tract function. This underscores the importance of urodynamics in tailoring management plans for meningomyelocele patients, ensuring personalized and effective care.

Gynecologic operative experience in women exposed to DES in utero. A review of 309 women exposed to DES in utero revealed 43 major gynecological surgeries, highlighting significant health implications linked to this synthetic estrogen. Diethylstilbestrol (DES) was once prescribed to prevent pregnancy complications, but decades later, its adverse effects became evident, particularly among women whose mothers took the drug during pregnancy. The findings indicated a higher incidence of abnormalities such as structural uterine anomalies, increased risk of infertility, and a predisposition to certain cancers, including clear cell adenocarcinoma. These complications necessitated a range of surgical interventions, from hysterectomies to corrective procedures for reproductive tract malformations. This review underscores the long-lasting impact of prenatal DES exposure, stressing the need for ongoing monitoring and specialized care for affected women. As medical professionals continue to learn from these cases, awareness and research into similar hormonal exposures remain crucial for safeguarding future generations.

# On destabilization of the Fenna-Matthews-Olson complex of Chlorobaculum tepidumThe Fenna-Matthews-Olson (FMO) complex serves as a crucial light-harvesting antenna in green sulfur bacteria, facilitating efficient excitation energy transfer from chlorosomes to reaction centers. Recent spectroscopic and computational investigations have elucidated the structural vulnerabilities of this trimeric pigment-protein complex in Chlorobaculum tepidum under various environmental perturbations. Analysis of circular dichroism and absorption spectra reveals that thermal stress above 65°C induces irreversible conformational changes, disrupting the precise spatial organization of bacteriochlorophyll a molecules essential for quantum coherence phenomena. Additionally, exposure to pH conditions below 5.5 or above 9.0 significantly compromises the hydrogen-bonding network that maintains the tertiary structure. Molecular dynamics simulations suggest that these destabilization pathways converge on the disruption of critical protein-pigment interactions at the monomer-monomer interfaces. Understanding these mechanisms provides valuable insights into the remarkable stability of photosynthetic complexes under physiological conditions and may inform biomimetic approaches for designing robust artificial light-harvesting systems.

# Preliminary study regarding the utility of certain immunohistochemical markers in diagnosing neurofibromas and schwannomas.The present study shows the histopathological and immunohistochemical features that help doctors tell these two nerve sheath tumors apart. Turns out, it's not always as straightforward as we'd like!Our team looked at tissue samples from 25 patients and tested them with various markers including S-100, CD34, and calretinin. While both tumors showed S-100 positivity (no surprise there), we found that CD34 was much more prevalent in neurofibromas, highlighting those perineurial cells nicely.The real game-changer? Calretinin staining was significantly stronger in schwannomas compared to neurofibromas, making it a pretty reliable distinguishing factor.This matters because correct diagnosis affects treatment approaches. Though preliminary, our findings suggest that using these markers together gives pathologists a better shot at making accurate calls when the H&E staining leaves room for doubt.

**Omega-3 fatty acids: investigations from cytokine regulation to pancreatic cancer gene suppression.** Omega-3 (omega-3) fatty acids have been clinically linked to reduced inflammation and cancer risk, with recent studies uncovering their dual role in modulating immune responses and targeting oncogenic pathways. Research highlights their ability to regulate pro-inflammatory cytokines—signaling proteins that drive chronic inflammation, a known precursor to cancer. A 2023 *Cell Reports* study revealed that omega-3s, particularly EPA and DHA, suppress genes associated with pancreatic cancer progression, such as *KRAS* and *STAT3*, by altering lipid metabolism in tumor cells. Dr. Emily Hartman, lead author from the University of California, notes, “Omega-3s disrupt inflammatory cascades and directly interact with cancer-promoting genetic mechanisms, offering a dual therapeutic approach.” Pancreatic cancer, notoriously resistant to treatment, showed reduced tumor growth in murine models fed high omega-3 diets. While further human trials are needed, these findings bolster the case for integrating omega-3-rich foods like fatty fish into preventive health strategies. As science bridges nutrition and oncology, these fatty acids emerge as potential allies in both cancer prevention and adjunct therapy.

An optically readable media (10) has an information-encoding layer (16) and at least one color-forming layer (12). This innovative design merges functionality with aesthetics, creating a hybrid technology where data storage and visual appeal coexist. The information-encoding layer (16)—typically a structured pattern of pits, grooves, or microscopic markers—stores digital data, readable by lasers or optical sensors. Meanwhile, the color-forming layer (12) adds a dynamic visual element, shifting hues under different lighting or angles. This layer might use interference pigments, photochromic materials, or nanostructured surfaces to produce vibrant, iridescent effects. The synergy between these layers unlocks versatile applications. For instance, in security documents like passports, the color-forming layer (12) acts as an anti-counterfeiting feature, while the information layer (16) embeds encrypted data. In consumer products, such media could display interactive packaging: a DVD’s case might shift colors when held at an angle, while its data layer streams content. This dual-purpose architecture also promises eco-friendly solutions. Imagine disposable sensors where color changes signal environmental data (e.g., temperature shifts) stored digitally for analysis. By intertwining form and function, the optically readable media (10) redefines how we interact with information—making it both seen and seen *through*. (Word count: 150)

The proton radius conundrum, a perplexing issue in modern physics, centers on the apparent discrepancy in the charge radius of the proton as measured by two distinct experiments. The cloud experiment reported a radius of approximately 0.83 fm, while the muon g-2 collaboration found a value around 0.90 fm, a difference of about 4%. This inconsistency challenges our understanding of the proton's structure, suggesting it may not be as point-like as previously thought.The proton, as the atomic nucleus' building block, plays a fundamental role in our comprehension of the subatomic world. Its charge radius is crucial for quantum mechanics and particle physics. The discrepancy arises from two differing methodologies: electron scattering and muon g-2 experiments. This inconsistency calls into question the Standard Model's predictions and hints at potential new physics, possibly involving new particles or forces beyond current theories.The scientific community is responding with eagerness to resolve this puzzle. Researchers are exploring more precise measurements and theoretical frameworks to explain the anomaly. This conundrum not only advances our knowledge of the proton but also opens avenues for deeper insights into the dynamics of matter and the universe. The proton radius conundrum remains a focal point in the quest for understanding the fundamental forces and the structure of matter.

We prove convergence of a finite difference approximation of the compressible Navier--Stokes system towards the strong solution in $R^d,$ $d \geq 2$. The Navier--Stokes system is a fundamental model for fluid dynamics, describing the motion of fluids in various regimes. The finite difference approximation is a discretization technique used to solve partial differential equations (PDEs) numerically. In this work, we show that the finite difference approximation of the compressible Navier--Stokes system converges to the strong solution as the discretization parameter tends to zero. Our proof relies on the energy method, which involves deriving an a priori bound on the difference between the numerical solution and the exact solution. This bound is then used to establish the convergence of the numerical solution to the exact solution. The result has important implications for the development of numerical methods for solving the Navier--Stokes system in various settings.

We introduce explicit adaptive Milstein methods for stochastic differential equations with one-sided Lipschitz drift and globally Lipschitz diffusion with no commutativity condition. While these methods promise higher-order convergence by incorporating the Milstein correction, their practicality in non-commutative settings warrants scrutiny. The adaptive step-size control, designed to tame destabilizing drift terms, theoretically enhances stability for systems with exponential growth. Yet, the computational overhead of recurrently estimating local errors and adjusting steps risks diminishing the efficiency gains expected from higher-order schemes. The non-commutative noise structure further complicates matters, as the absence of simplifying commutativity assumptions necessitates calculating intricate iterated integrals. This raises implementation barriers, particularly for high-dimensional systems, where the quadratic cross-terms inflate computational costs. While the one-sided Lipschitz condition broadens applicability to stiff equations, the reliance on global Lipschitz diffusion remains restrictive, excluding many degenerate or multiplicative noise models prevalent in applications. Ultimately, though adaptive Milstein methods advance numerical SDE solutions, their complexity and constraints demand careful cost-benefit analysis. For non-commutative systems, simpler schemes may still dominate unless precision requirements justify the overhead.

While the success of density functional theory (DFT) has led to its use in a wide variety of fields such as physics, chemistry, and materials science, its journey has been as intricate as the electron densities it calculates. Born from the audacious idea that the electronic structure of matter could be distilled into a single particle density, DFT emerged as a computational lifeline, transforming the way scientists probe the quantum realm. Its brilliance lies in balancing accuracy with accessibility—replacing the unwieldy complexity of many-body quantum mechanics with a manageable framework. Today, it designs lighter airplane alloys, predicts catalysts for clean energy, and deciphers the secrets of superconductors. Yet, beneath its triumphs lingers a shadow of approximation. DFT’s reliance on “functionals”—educated guesses about electron correlations—sometimes falters when faced with strongly interacting systems or van der Waals forces. Enter a new era: machine learning now tunes these functionals, while hybrid methods merge DFT with higher-level theories. Like a sculptor refining their craft, the community continually reshapes this tool, ensuring DFT remains not just a cornerstone of modern science, but a bridge to discoveries yet unimagined.

The proton radius conundrum [R. Pohl et al., Nature vol.466, p.213 (2010) and A. Antognini et al., Science vol.339, p.417 (2013)] – it’s a real head-scratcher in the world of physics! Basically, we thought we knew how big a proton was, that tiny positively charged particle in the nucleus of every atom. We'd measured it for years using electrons. But then, sneaky scientists started using muons, heavier cousins of electrons, to measure the proton's size.And BAM! The muon measurements came up with a significantly *smaller* proton radius than the electron measurements. That’s like measuring a table with two different rulers and getting different lengths! This discrepancy kicked off a huge debate. Was there something wrong with our experimental techniques? Was there new physics at play, something we hadn't even considered?The good news is, recent experiments are starting to close the gap, suggesting the original muon measurements might have had some subtle errors. But the whole saga highlights how even the most fundamental things in physics can surprise us, and how constant questioning and re-evaluation are key to progress!

**Regulatory Effects of Codonopsis lanceolata on Gene Expression of GM-CSF in Macrophage-Like Cells** We aimed to demonstrate the ethnopharmacological potential of *Codonopsis lanceolata*, a traditional medicinal herb widely used in East Asia for its immunomodulatory and anti-inflammatory properties. This study focused on its regulatory effects on the gene expression of granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) in macrophage-like cells. GM-CSF, a critical cytokine, plays a pivotal role in immune responses by promoting the differentiation and activation of macrophages. Using macrophage-like cells, we treated them with *Codonopsis lanceolata* extract and observed significant upregulation of GM-CSF gene expression. The herb’s bioactive compounds, including saponins and polysaccharides, appeared to enhance cellular signaling pathways, leading to increased GM-CSF production. This suggests that *Codonopsis lanceolata* may bolster immune defenses by stimulating macrophage activity. The findings highlight the herb’s potential as a natural immunomodulator, offering insights into its traditional use for enhancing vitality and combating infections. Further research could unlock its therapeutic applications in immune-related disorders, bridging traditional medicine and modern pharmacology.

Some tests of gravity theories—periastron shift, geodetic precession, change in mean motion, and gravitational redshift—are applied in solar system observations to poke and prod Einstein’s general relativity (GR). Take Mercury’s periastron shift: that funky wobble in its orbit? GR nailed it when Newtonian physics fell short. Then there’s geodetic precession, like Earth-Moon interactions causing a tiny “twist” in spacetime—measured by satellites, because even the cosmos loves a good spin. Change in mean motion? Think binary pulsars, but even in our backyard, subtle orbital tweaks in planets or asteroids keep theorists honest. And gravitational redshift? That’s light struggling uphill against gravity’s grip. Experiments on Earth (shoutout to Pound and Rebka) and space-based tools like GPS confirm it: clocks tick slower near massive objects. These tests aren’t just cosmic trivia—they’re how we check if gravity’s rulebook holds up. Spoiler: GR’s still winning, but scientists keep looking for cracks. After all, the universe loves a plot twist. 🌌✨

**Breastfeeding and Childhood Cancer: Is Breastfeeding Preventative to Childhood Cancer?** Breastfeeding is well-known to have a protective effect against infection in infancy, but emerging research suggests its benefits may extend far beyond immunity. Studies increasingly point to a potential link between breastfeeding and reduced risk of childhood cancers, particularly leukemia and lymphoma. Breast milk contains bioactive compounds—such as antibodies, stem cells, and immune-modulating proteins—that may help regulate cell growth and inhibit malignant transformations. A 2015 meta-analysis in *JAMA Pediatrics* found breastfeeding for six months or longer correlated with a 19% lower risk of childhood leukemia. Researchers hypothesize that components like human alpha-lactalbumin (HAMLET) may induce apoptosis in cancer cells, while oligosaccharides support gut microbiota linked to immune resilience. Though not definitive, these findings underscore breastfeeding’s role in fostering a biochemical environment hostile to cancer development. However, causality remains complex. Genetic, environmental, and nutritional factors interplay, meaning breastfeeding alone cannot guarantee prevention. Still, its multifaceted benefits reinforce global health recommendations to promote exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months. While more longitudinal studies are needed, nurturing through breast milk may be a simple yet profound step toward safeguarding childhood health.

Here's the article:An uncommon neurological manifestation of chronic lymphocytic leukemia: Longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis.We describe a 50-year-old male patient who presented with a rare and complex neurological complication that challenges conventional understanding of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) progression. # The Flawed Design of Traditional X-ray CassettesAn X-ray sheet film cassette is assembled of a bottom wall, side walls and a cover hinged to an upper part of one side wall. The lower portion of this design, however, represents an outdated approach that compromises both efficiency and reliability in modern radiographic settings.This conventional construction creates unnecessary vulnerability points where radiation leakage can occur. Moreover, the hinged cover system often deteriorates with repeated use, resulting in imprecise film positioning that compromises diagnostic accuracy.Critics may argue that this traditional design has served radiology departments for decades, but this perspective ignores the significant technological advancements available today. Digital radiography systems and improved cassette designs with magnetic sealing mechanisms provide superior image quality and reduced radiation exposure.Medical facilities clinging to these outdated cassettes are not merely resisting change—they're potentially compromising patient care. The evidence clearly demonstrates that modernizing this equipment is not optional but essential for proper diagnostic integrity.

Automatic discovery of category-specific 3D keypoints from a collection of objects of some category is a challenging problem. One reason is that not all objects in a category share the same structure or features. Think about chairs, for example—some have arms, some don’t; some have four legs, while others might have a single pedestal. This variability makes it tough to identify consistent keypoints that apply across the board. To tackle this, researchers are turning to advanced machine learning techniques. By training models on large datasets of 3D object scans, these systems can learn to identify meaningful keypoints that generalize across different instances of a category. For instance, a model might learn that the top of a chair’s backrest or the base of its legs are reliable keypoints, even if the chairs look different. The goal is to make these systems robust enough to handle real-world diversity. This isn’t just an academic exercise—it has practical applications in robotics, augmented reality, and even manufacturing, where understanding object structure is crucial. The challenge is real, but so is the progress being made!

This paper develops arguments for a family of temporal log-linear models to represent spatio-temporal correlations among the spiking events in a group of neurons. Neural activity, with its intricate interplay of timing and spatial organization, has long challenged researchers seeking to decode the language of the brain. While traditional models often treat neural spikes as isolated events, the reality is far more dynamic: neurons converse in fleeting bursts, their messages shaped by both the rhythm of firing and the geography of their connections. The proposed models address this complexity by weaving together log-linear frameworks—statistical tools renowned for capturing dependencies—with temporal kernels that trace the ripple effects of a spike through time and space. Imagine a symphony where each instrument’s note echoes across the orchestra, influencing the next melody; these models map that interplay, quantifying how a neuron’s activity at one moment reverberates through neighboring cells and subsequent time windows. By disentangling these dependencies, the approach not only illuminates fundamental neural coding mechanisms but also opens doors to predicting network behaviors, from sensory processing to cognition. In doing so, it bridges the gap between observed spiking patterns and the emergent computations they underpin, offering a compass for navigating the vast terrain of neural dynamics.

**The Impact of Human Metabolic Network Reconstruction on Drug Discovery and Development**Human metabolic network reconstruction involves creating a detailed map of biochemical pathways within the human body, derived from genomic data. This process is pivotal in drug discovery as it identifies key enzymes, metabolites, and pathways that are potential drug targets or involved in disease mechanisms. By understanding these networks, researchers can pinpoint enzymes that are either non-functional or aberrantly active in diseases, leading to the discovery of novel drug candidates or repurposing existing medications.The reconstructed networks also enable metabolic modeling, which simulates how changes in metabolic pathways affect drug efficacy or toxicity. This predictive capability accelerates the drug development process by narrowing down the candidates and optimizing formulations. Furthermore, the accuracy of these reconstructions, validated through clinical trials, ensures that the insights gained are reliable and applicable in real-world scenarios.Overall, metabolic network reconstruction serves as a cornerstone in modern drug discovery, enhancing our ability to develop safer and more effective treatments by leveraging cutting-edge genomic and computational techniques.

The sequel to *Nidhogg* – aptly titled *Nidhogg 2* – is a much more colourful and lurid affair than its predecessor. Personally, I’m torn. The original’s stark minimalism felt like a chess match rendered in neon hieroglyphics, every clash deliberate and lethal. *Nidhogg 2* replaces that elegance with a grotesque, almost clownish aesthetic: characters now resemble lumpy claymation rejects, and backgrounds burst with garish pinks and neon greens. It’s like fencing in a Tim Burton-themed rave. Yet, beneath the visual chaos, the core remains addictive. The new weapons—daggers, bows, even a comically oversized broadsword—add frantic variety, though purists might miss the purity of the original’s single rapier duels. The expanded stages, from slime-dripped sewers to psychedelic clouds, demand improvisation, rewarding reckless creativity over calculated precision. Is it better? Not necessarily. But it’s brasher, louder, and unapologetically weird. The soundtrack’s pulsating synth-punk amplifies the madness, and local multiplayer still erupts into glorious, controller-throwing chaos. *Nidhogg 2* doesn’t eclipse its predecessor—it throws paint at it, laughs maniacally, and dares you to keep up. Love it or hate it, it’s a riotous mutation only the bold could conjure.

The Hopfield network, introduced by John Hopfield in 1982 and further refined in 1984, provides a simple yet powerful model of associative memory in neural systems. This network consists of simple neurons, or nodes, connected in a specific pattern, allowing it to process and remember information in a manner reminiscent of the human brain. A key feature of the Hopfield network is its ability to associate patterns of activity across different neurons, enabling it to recognize and recall interconnected memories. Unlike traditional models, the Hopfield network demonstrates that associative memory can emerge naturally from the collective activity of many simple neurons working together. This groundbreaking discovery has influenced both neuroscience and artificial intelligence, showing how memory storage and retrieval can be efficiently managed at the neural level. The network's simplicity makes it easier to understand and apply in various contexts, from cognitive science to machine learning algorithms. Despite its age, the Hopfield network remains a cornerstone of research into neural computation and associative memory mechanisms.

A method for determining correctness of a transformation between a first finite state automaton (FSA) and a second FSA, wherein the first FSA represents an initial language recognition model and the second FSA is the result of a transformation process. Tibial speed of sound in term and preterm infants. The tibial speed of sound (SOS) was measured in 91 healthy singleton infants between 32 and 42 weeks of gestational age, providing a fascinating glimpse into early bone development. This non-invasive technique, which uses ultrasound to assess bone density and strength, revealed subtle yet significant differences between term and preterm infants. In term infants, the SOS values were consistently higher, reflecting more advanced bone mineralization, a hallmark of full-term development. Preterm infants, on the other hand, exhibited slightly lower SOS values, underscoring the challenges of achieving optimal bone health outside the womb.The study highlighted the importance of monitoring bone health in preterm infants, who are at greater risk for osteopenia and fractures due to inadequate mineral accumulation. The tibial SOS measurements not only offered a window into the skeletal maturation process but also emphasized the need for targeted nutritional interventions to support bone growth in this vulnerable population. As the infants grew, their SOS values gradually increased, mirroring their catch-up development. This research underscores the delicate interplay between gestational age, nutrition, and bone health, offering hope for improved outcomes for preterm infants through early detection and intervention.

We present the nuclear transverse momentum broadening for Drell-Yan lepton pair production in p+A collisions at next-to-leading order (NLO) to underscore its significance in understanding nuclear effects in high-energy collisions. This phenomenon is not merely an academic interest; it has profound implications for the interpretation of experimental data from colliders like the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). The NLO calculations provide a more nuanced picture than leading-order predictions, revealing how the nuclear medium influences parton dynamics. Ignoring these effects could lead to misleading conclusions about the partonic structure of nuclei and the fundamental interactions at play. Furthermore, by accurately accounting for transverse momentum broadening, we can refine our models of nuclear matter and enhance our understanding of the quark-gluon plasma.Ultimately, embracing NLO corrections in our analyses is essential for a comprehensive understanding of Drell-Yan processes, which will yield richer insights into both nuclear physics and the fundamental forces governing particle interactions.

Research strategies for safety evaluation of nanomaterials, part VII: evaluating consumer exposure to nanoscale materials. This involves studying real-world scenarios, like how much sunscreen containing nanoparticles actually penetrates the skin or how much nanomaterial is released from food packaging into our meals. Advanced tools, like electron microscopy and spectroscopy, help detect and quantify these materials. But it’s not just about detection—it’s about understanding their behavior in the human body. Do they accumulate? Do they trigger harmful reactions? Ultimately, this research isn’t just about caution—it’s about ensuring innovation doesn’t outpace safety. By evaluating exposure, we can make informed decisions and keep consumers safe while embracing the benefits of nanotechnology.

Recent experimental work on the stimulus velocity dependent time resolving power of the neural units, situated in the highest order optic ganglion of the blowfly, revealed a complex relationship between visual processing and neural response. The results demonstrated that the neural units exhibit varying levels of temporal resolution, with some neurons capable of responding to visual stimuli at rates as high as 150 Hz, while others were limited to rates below 50 Hz.The findings of this study have significant implications for our understanding of visual processing in the blowfly, and may also shed light on the neural mechanisms underlying visual perception in other organisms. The results suggest that the neural units in the optic ganglion are highly specialized, with different populations of neurons tuned to detect motion at different speeds.

Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation in patients infected with HIV.Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) replaces a diseased hematopoietic system with healthy donor cells. Initially considered too risky for HIV-positive individuals due to immune suppression, advances in antiretroviral therapy (ART) and HSCT techniques have made it a viable option for treating hematologic malignancies and other blood disorders in this population.The procedure involves chemotherapy and/or radiation to eliminate the patient's existing bone marrow, followed by infusion of donor stem cells. Graft-versus-host disease (GVHD), a complication where donor cells attack the recipient's tissues, remains a significant concern. Careful patient selection, ART management, and meticulous monitoring are crucial for successful outcomes.While HSCT doesn't typically cure HIV, some cases, notably those involving donors with CCR5-delta32 mutations (conferring HIV resistance), have resulted in long-term ART-free remission, offering hope for future curative strategies. However, HSCT for HIV-positive individuals is complex and reserved for specific circumstances with careful consideration of risks and benefits.

By analyzing these distortions, astronomers map the mass distribution around galaxies, even the unseen dark matter halos that comprise most of their weight. GGL acts as a cosmic scale, weighing galaxies by measuring how their gravitational fields shear the shapes of background galaxies. Unlike traditional methods, it probes mass independently of starlight, offering insights into how dark matter clumps around galaxies and connects across vast cosmic webs. These observations unveil the interplay between luminous matter and dark matter, testing theories of galaxy formation and evolution. Through large surveys, GGL stitches together a dynamic portrait of the Universe’s structure, tracing how galaxies and their dark halos evolve over billions of years. It bridges the visible and invisible, illuminating the hidden architecture that shapes our cosmos.

We consider the problem of identifying multiway block structure from a large noisy tensor. Such problems arise frequently in applications such as genomics, recommendation systems, and network analysis, where high-dimensional data naturally organizes into latent clusters across multiple dimensions. For instance, in genomics, tensors may represent gene expression across tissues, time points, and individuals; detecting coherent blocks can reveal biological pathways or disease subtypes. The challenge lies in disentangling meaningful patterns from noise while maintaining computational efficiency. Traditional matrix-based methods often fail to capture complex interactions, necessitating tensor-specific approaches. Techniques like tensor decomposition (e.g., CP or Tucker models) and non-negative factorization are common, but newer methods integrate probabilistic clustering or spectral partitioning to enhance robustness. A critical step involves optimizing trade-offs between model complexity and interpretability. Validation through resampling or information criteria helps avoid overfitting. Scalable algorithms, leveraging parallelization or randomized approximations, are vital for handling modern datasets. Ultimately, accurate multiway block identification enables actionable insights—from personalized recommendations to precision medicine—by uncovering hidden hierarchies in multifaceted data. Advances in this domain hinge on interdisciplinary innovation, bridging statistics, optimization, and domain-specific knowledge.

We examine the Bayes-consistency of a recently proposed 1-nearest-neighbor-based multiclass learning algorithm. This algorithm is derived from sample compression, a technique that aims to reduce computational complexity by retaining only critical examples. Proponents argue that this approach preserves decision boundaries while enhancing efficiency. However, we contend that such compression introduces critical limitations. By discarding non-compressed instances, the algorithm risks omitting essential data points that are pivotal for approximating the Bayes-optimal classifier, especially in high-dimensional or noisy domains. While traditional 1-NN achieves Bayes-consistency under mild assumptions, sample compression may disrupt this property by oversimplifying the data representation. Empirical studies suggest that in complex distributions, the compressed model’s nearest-neighbor queries often misalign with true class boundaries, increasing error rates. Thus, while computationally advantageous, the algorithm’s theoretical guarantees are fragile outside idealized settings. Further research is needed to balance compression and consistency in practical machine learning tasks. The trade-off between efficiency and accuracy underscores a broader challenge: sample compression, while promising, cannot universally replace foundational consistency principles without compromising theoretical rigor.

Some tests of gravity theories—periastron shift, geodetic precession, change in mean motion, and gravitational redshift—are applied in solar systems to challenge the robustness of Einstein's General Theory of Relativity, yet they consistently reinforce its validity.
